Manna from an invasive tree

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How a pest choking South Africa's drylands is being transformed into jobs, hope - and a roasted caffeine free drink.

Unique Selling Point:
It's one of South Africa's most destructive invasive trees....chocking the land, draining precious water, and costing millions to eradicate. But in the Karoo town of Calvinia, it's become something else entirely. Once a year, hundreds of residents harvest its seedpods - turning a pest into income, dignity, and survival. Now one man is taking it even further - transforming an environmental disaster into a globally exported coffee.

Summary:
In March every year the quiet Karoo town of Calvinia comes alive as hundreds of residents harvest seedpods from one of South Africa’s most destructive invasive alien trees: the Mesquite.
Introduced over a century ago as a drought solution, the Mesquite has since spread uncontrollably, draining groundwater and infesting more than eight million hectares of land in the Northern Cape. While government eradication programmes struggle to contain it, one entrepreneur believes the tree might offer an alternative solution.
We follow the unlikely journey of Mesquite seedpods — from township streets where pensioners and unemployed residents collect them for cash, to a Somerset West factory where they are roasted and ground into the world’s only Mesquite coffee, now exported internationally.
At the centre of the story is Brandt Coetzee, whose decades-long relationship with the tree has evolved from furniture-making to nutraceuticals, and finally to coffee. His operation employs nearly 700 seasonal harvesters in Calvinia alone, providing a critical income stream for people living on government pensions.
The story also revisits the tree’s complicated past through farmers who once relied on it as livestock feed — and now live with the unintended consequences of its spread. It examines whether commercialising an invasive species can realistically curb its expansion, or whether it risks entrenching the problem further.

Story Overview
In March, harvest season begins. Residents — many surviving on government pensions — scour the town and surrounding veld for Mesquite seedpods. For some, it means food on the table. For others, it means dignity, purpose, and community.
Community leader Donavan du Plooy calls it “Christmas in March,” earning up to R8,000 for a ton of pods while sharing profits with helpers.
Yet the Mesquite’s legacy is complex. Farmers like Hennie Visagie, now in his seventies, remember when the tree was deliberately planted — watered by hand — and celebrated as “mother’s milk” for livestock during droughts. That same tree now infests more than 8 million hectares in the Northern Cape alone.
Government eradication programmes like Working for Water have struggled to keep pace. Coetzee’s approach is different: instead of cutting it down, harvest the seedpods before they spread — and pay people to do it.

Key Themes
Environmental unintended consequences

Innovation born from scarcity

Job creation in rural South Africa

Sustainability versus eradication

Why It Matters
Manna from an Invasive Tree is a uniquely South African story with global relevance — blending science, environment, economics, and human resilience. It challenges conventional conservation thinking while asking hard questions about long-term ecological responsibility.
The story combines strong characters, striking visuals, and ethical complexity. It reveals how forgotten communities adapt to environmental crises, and whether hope can be found in the most unlikely places.

Script:


Final Script: Manna from an Invasive Tree
Date: 31 March 2026
Duration: 10 minutes

UPSound: Music over visuals: Wide Karoo landscape, scorched earth stretching to the horizon.

VO1 This is Namaqualand in the Northern Cape, where the land stretches as far as the eye can see. Temperatures can soar to 50 degrees, and trees are scarce.
UPsound: sheep under the tree bleating
VO2 In terrain this harsh, sheep farming is a lifeline — but when drought strips the veld bare, they have to make another plan.
UPSound: Erin getting out of bakkie and opening the gate.
VO3 A century ago, a drought-resistant tree from the Americas — the Mesquite — was introduced to provide shade from the unforgiving sun, and its seedpods became a vital source of feed for livestock.
HENNIE VISAGIE: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated): Ek was klein toe hulle die bome aangeplant het…maar dit het gesukkel. In die begin het hy nie maklik gegroei nie. (I was small when they planted the trees. Initially they struggled to grow.)
VO4: Hennie Visagie, a sheep farmer from the Calvinia district, remembers when the trees took root...and when the first seedpods fell - like manna from heaven.
HENNIE VISAGIE: SHEEP FARMER: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated): Dis, soos n man nou sal se, moedersmelk. Ek meen, dis vir hulle, jy sien mos self die skaap gesien hulle is mooi. Die kos is nie volop nie…..so hulle geniet dit. (It’s like mother’s milk. As you can see, the sheep are well fed….so they enjoy it.)

VO5 But, there was a cost. The seeds passed through livestock undigested…spreading into dry riverbeds, taking hold across the landscape.

UPSound music

LINK: Around me is one of South Africa’s most aggressive invasive species — the Mesquite tree. It was planted here more than a century ago as a drought solution. But today, it covers millions of hectares, draining scarce groundwater and costing a fortune to try and control.

UPsound music

ERIN: At what point did the blessing of the Mesquite started feeling like a problem?

HENNIE VISAGIE: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated): Dis al n klompie jare terug. Hier is manne wat hul plaas skoon het veral ouens wat nou hier is op klein skaal, manna wat uit die rivier uit water lei, vloedvlaktes en damme het wat hulle vloedbesprooing doen. So hulle wil nie graag die bome op hulle land he nie. So hy het maar sy probleme. (A good few years ago already. There are farmers here who have cleared their land — especially those who draw water from the river, who have floodplains and dams and use flood irrigation — so they don’t want the trees on their land. So it does have its problems.)

ERIN: What are they?

HENNIE VISAGIE: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated): Hy maak jou goeie veld tot niet omdat hy in a waterryke area groei. Automaties het jy in jou vloedvlak waar jy beter kos het. (It destroys your good grazing land because it grows in water-rich areas. Naturally, it takes over your floodplains where you have better grazing)

VO6 And once it takes hold, it spreads fast.
BRANDT COETZEE: Like an average tree of around about two and a half meter, use roundabout 60 liters of water per day.
VO7 Brandt Coetzee grew up in Prieska in the Northern Cape. He first encountered the Mesquite in the 1990s, when the government began clearing invasive species in the area — and he knows the damaging impacts all too well.
BRANDT COETZEE: Entrepreneur: You can just imagine how much of the precious underground water of the Northern Cape is sucked up by this trees.
VO8 But where others saw a problem, Brandt saw potential — a way these invasive trees could ease the economic strain on the people who live here.
BRANDT COETZEE: I really prayed for an answer because I know we sit with such a big problem that there's not a solution to that.
VO9 Knowing the nutritional value it offered livestock, he first turned the pods into a superfood — but it barely dented the spread. He knew it needed something bigger - and then came an experiment.
ERIN: Take me back to that moment in the kitchen with the smoke and roasting the pods with your son.
BRANDT COETZEE: We’ve got some of the seed pods on the oven, and we roasted it, and it was just smoke. But it was like a lightbulb moment. And I know it was divine, because I couldn't think of something like that.

UPSound Factory shots

VO10 That moment led to a roasted, caffeine-free drink — made from the seedpods, known for their natural sugars, fiber and protein.

UPSound: [Erin]: It’s quite special to drink this in Calvinia.

[Brandt Coetzee]: It is. It is. Cheers!

Erin: Cheers!.......It’s very malty, caramel, vanilla, nut…

Brandt Coetzee: And you will also taste a little bit of sweetness coming through.

VO11 But the real story isn’t in the product. It’s in the people. And once a year, in Calvinia, that moment comes to life.
UPSound People picking up seedpods
VO12 From January to March, when the trees drop their pods, locals head out with bags as the excitement of the harvest takes hold. Some even call it Christmas in March.
DONAVAN DU PLOOY: There’s no Santa Claus coming because you notice we don’t have a lot of chimneys, so I think he skips us, but something like festive season.
VO13 In a place where jobs are scarce, harvesting the Mesquite brings hope – and cash in hand.
UPSound factory sound
Donavan du Plooy helps guide the harvest and supports locals with transport and storage.

UPSound - (Afikaans, subtitled/translation): Donavan du Plooy: Is die net al julle sakke wat julle gebring het? (Are these all the bags you brought?)
DONAVAN DU PLOOY: HARVESTER: I look at the pod. I look at the story and at what could possibly happen, and the endless possibilities of having hope that something better can come out of this thing.
UPSound seedpods placed into crates

LINK: We’re at the collection point in town and there is huge activity and anticipation. Locals have been coming in since daybreak with sacks of seedpods and there is such excitement, because these bags get exchanged for cash in hand.

UPSound natural factory buzz

JAMES MAMPA: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated) Calvinia trek maar net bietjie swaar en so aan….die werksomstandighede…. ons kry maar net n bietjie swaar. Ons kry nie meer werk ok nie. (Calvinia is tough…there isn’t much work. That’s why we struggle.)
VO14 For first-time harvesters like James Mampa, it’s a chance to earn something, however small.
[ERIN]: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated) En hoeveel geld gaan jy kry? (How much will you get today?)

[JAMES MAMPA]: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated) Ek moet nou maar kyk, dat ek vir my n broodjie koop. (I'll have to see …..enough to buy a loaf of bread.)

UPSound people queueing

[ERIN]: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated) Is die mense opgewonde? (Are the people excited?)

JAMES MAMPA: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translated) Ja, ja, ja. Kyk hoe staan hulle hier. (Yes, yes, yes….look how they’re lining up.)

VO15 From the queues to the weighing scale, the collection point hums with a strong sense of community. For regulars like Dawid Matthys, it’s part of the rhythm of the season — and today, he’s hoping his harvest pays off.

UPSound: [Erin]: How many kilos was it all together Brandt?

Brandt Coetzee: It was 76.4 kilograms.

[Erin] 76.4 kilogram?

Brandt Coetzee: ... .and it was four-hundred-and-fifty-nine rand.

[Erin]: Wow! You know he has been harvesting since December.

Brandt Coetzee: As soon as the pods start falling these guys start to collect because they want to get to the pods before the animals or the rain.

[Erin]: (English/Afrikaans translation): Is jy tevrede met jou kontant? Are you satisfied with your cash?

Dawid Matthys: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translation): Ek is tevrede. Ek het n nuwe baba. Ek het nog wat ek moet bring. Ek is bietjie haastig. (I am satisfied. I have a new baby. I have more to bring. I am a bit in a hurry.)

[Erin]: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translation): Vir die vrou en die baba. (For the wife and the baby.)

Dawid Matthys: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translation) Dis reg. That’s right.

[Erin]: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translation) Geluk Dawid. Congratulations Dawid!

Brandt Coetzee: (Afrikaans, subtitled/translation): Dankie Dawid. Thank you Dawid.

UPSound music and factory sounds

VO16 Small returns - that quickly add up.
Pause
This season, Donavan and his team collected more than 11 tonnes.

DONAVAN DU PLOOY: You know there's something that they call in South Africa, we call it ‘Januarie’, and now it’s ‘Februarie’. Now, we don't have worries, because we know we're going to pick up the ‘peels’, and it’s going to give us this, this boost.
UPSound music
VO17 From the foothills of the Hantam mountains, the Mesquite is being reimagined.
UPSound music

BRANDT COETZEE: To really make an impact in nature; to stop the spread of the trees; to create jobs on a long-term basis for the people of the Northern Cape - that is my long-term goal. That is my vision and that’s what I live for every day.
DONAVAN DU PLOOY: I would call it hope, in a nutshell. It’s a hopeful story. Invasive specie falling from the tree, and out of this something comes. And I feel that is a hopeful thing.
LINK In the Karoo, survival has always meant making the most of the land. The Mesquite tree was once planted in hope, later feared as a mistake. It’s still controversial — but here, when the seedpods fall, they don’t just hit the ground… they lift a community.
___________________________________________________________________________________________________________

ON-CAMERA LINK:
Across South Africa, one invasive tree is choking the land, spreading faster than anyone expected…
UPSOUND – Brandt Coetzee:
The number of pods in tonnage….it is just unthinkable.
ON-CAMERA:

It’s Christmas in March. And so you can go out and spoil yourself. And that gives hope.

VO Once a year in a small town in the Karoo, hundreds of people head into the veld - harvesting seedpods from an invasive tree ... .turning a pest into income.
UPSound: [Erin]: How many kilos was it all together?

Brandt Coetzee: It was 76.4 kilogram..and it was four-hundred-and-fifty-nine rand.

VO And an environmental disaster into hope.
__________________________________________________________________________________________________________

VO Can an invasive species really become part of the solution?
UPSound - Brandt Coetzee: We’ll run out of hands before we run out of product.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): How a pest choking South Africa's drylands is being transformed into jobs, hope - and a roasted caffeine free drink.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's one of South Africa's most destructive invasive trees....chocking the land, draining precious water, and costing millions to eradicate. But in the Karoo town of Calvinia, it's become something else entirely. Once a year, hundreds of residents harvest its seedpods - turning a pest into income, dignity, and survival. Now one man is taking it even further - transforming an environmental disaster into a globally exported coffee.
metadata.Summary: In March every year the quiet Karoo town of Calvinia comes alive as hundreds of residents harvest seedpods from one of South Africa’s most destructive invasive alien trees: the Mesquite. Introduced over a century ago as a drought solution, the Mesquite has since spread uncontrollably, draining groundwater and infesting more than eight million hectares of land in the Northern Cape. While government eradication programmes struggle to contain it, one entrepreneur believes the tree might offer an alternative solution. We follow the unlikely journey of Mesquite seedpods — from township streets where pensioners and unemployed residents collect them for cash, to a Somerset West factory where they are roasted and ground into the world’s only Mesquite coffee, now exported internationally. At the centre of the story is Brandt Coetzee, whose decades-long relationship with the tree has evolved from furniture-making to nutraceuticals, and finally to coffee. His operation employs nearly 700 seasonal harvesters in Calvinia alone, providing a critical income stream for people living on government pensions. The story also revisits the tree’s complicated past through farmers who once relied on it as livestock feed — and now live with the unintended consequences of its spread. It examines whether commercialising an invasive species can realistically curb its expansion, or whether it risks entrenching the problem further. Story Overview In March, harvest season begins. Residents — many surviving on government pensions — scour the town and surrounding veld for Mesquite seedpods. For some, it means food on the table. For others, it means dignity, purpose, and community. Community leader Donavan du Plooy calls it “Christmas in March,” earning up to R8,000 for a ton of pods while sharing profits with helpers. Yet the Mesquite’s legacy is complex. Farmers like Hennie Visagie, now in his seventies, remember when the tree was deliberately planted — watered by hand — and celebrated as “mother’s milk” for livestock during droughts. That same tree now infests more than 8 million hectares in the Northern Cape alone. Government eradication programmes like Working for Water have struggled to keep pace. Coetzee’s approach is different: instead of cutting it down, harvest the seedpods before they spread — and pay people to do it. Key Themes Environmental unintended consequences Innovation born from scarcity Job creation in rural South Africa Sustainability versus eradication Why It Matters Manna from an Invasive Tree is a uniquely South African story with global relevance — blending science, environment, economics, and human resilience. It challenges conventional conservation thinking while asking hard questions about long-term ecological responsibility. The story combines strong characters, striking visuals, and ethical complexity. It reveals how forgotten communities adapt to environmental crises, and whether hope can be found in the most unlikely places.
